core: Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE): Bronze Age civilization, ritual bronze vessels, oracle bones and the earliest systematic Chinese writing
Zhou dynasty (1046-256 BCE): overthrow of the Shang at Muye, the Mandate of Heaven, longest-lasting dynasty
Mandate of Heaven: divine sanction to rule contingent on just, moral government, and forfeitable — basis of the dynastic-cycle idea
Hundred Schools of Thought during the Eastern Zhou; the founding of Confucianism and Daoism and the philosophy of Legalism (named with period)
Qin unification under the first emperor in 221 BCE: standardization of script, currency, weights and measures; connecting walls into an early Great Wall; Terracotta Army
Han dynasty (202 BCE-220 CE): founding by Liu Bang, long and influential era, opening of Silk Road trade under Emperor Wu
Major inventions over time: silk, paper (Cai Lun, c. 105 CE), and the magnetic compass (lodestone divination in Han era, navigational use by the Song)
supporting: Geography: Yellow (Huang He) and Yangtze river valleys as the cradle of Chinese civilization
Battle of Muye (1046 BCE) and the fall of the Shang
Confucius (Kongzi), c. 551-479 BCE, as founding figure of Confucianism
Legalism as the governing ideology adopted by the Qin state

claims.claim: The Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE) was a Bronze Age civilization in the Yellow River region whose signature achievements were ritual bronze casting and the earliest systematic Chinese writing, preserved on oracle bones used for divination.
Oracle-bone script (jiaguwen), inscribed on tortoise shells and animal bones and dating from roughly the fourteenth to eleventh century BCE, is the earliest known form of systematic Chinese writing.
The Zhou overthrew the Shang around 1046 BCE (at the Battle of Muye) and founded the Zhou dynasty (1046-256 BCE), the longest-lasting dynasty in Chinese history.

The Zhou introduced the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that Heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler and can withdraw it from an unjust or incompetent one — a doctrine that justified dynastic change and shaped the Chinese concept of the dynastic cycle.

During the later Zhou centuries the 'Hundred Schools of Thought' flourished, producing Confucianism (founded on the teachings of Confucius, c. 551-479 BCE), Daoism, and Legalism, which grounded governmental power in a strict written legal code of rewards and punishments.

The Qin unified China in 221 BCE under its first emperor (Qin Shi Huang), who standardized the writing system, coinage, and law, connected existing defensive walls into an early Great Wall, and was buried with the Terracotta Army.

The Han dynasty (202 BCE-220 CE), founded by the commoner Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu) after the Qin collapse, was a long and influential era; under Emperor Wu the Silk Road trade routes to the west were opened, associated with the envoy Zhang Qian (missions 138-126 BCE).

Chinese inventions developed over time include silk, paper (a fine paper-making process credited to Cai Lun, c. 105 CE, during the Han), and the magnetic compass, which began as a lodestone divination instrument and was developed into a navigational device only later, by the Song dynasty.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Founding date of the Han dynasty
positions: 202 BCE, when Liu Bang defeated Xiang Yu and was proclaimed emperor (World History Encyclopedia)
206 BCE, dated from the fall of the Qin and Liu Bang's assumption of the title King of Han (OpenStax and many textbooks)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson dates the Han to 202 BCE (Liu Bang's accession as emperor) while noting that 206 BCE is commonly given for the founding, measured from the Qin collapse. Both are standard; the four-year gap is the interregnum of civil war.

conflictingEvidence.issue: End date of the Shang / start of the Zhou
positions: Shang ends c. 1046 BCE at the Battle of Muye (World History Encyclopedia, Metropolitan Museum chronology)
OpenStax rounds the transition to c. 1050 BCE
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Uses c. 1046 BCE, the widely cited conventional date for the Zhou conquest, noting the figure is approximate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Attribution of 'the compass' to the Han dynasty
positions: Popular lists (including World History Encyclopedia's Han timeline) credit the Han with 'the compass'
Historians of technology distinguish early Han lodestone divination boards from the magnetic navigational compass, which is documented only from the Song dynasty (Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays, 1088)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the compass as an invention that developed over time: lodestone divination in the Han era, navigational use by the Song. It does not claim the Han invented a navigational compass.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Any precise single-year framing of philosophical 'founding' dates beyond Confucius's conventional lifespan was avoided as unverifiable to a year.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate generalities in the generated draft with verified date ranges and named dynasties, and separated the lodestone/divination origin of the compass from its later navigational form to avoid a common oversimplification.

CC BY, but lesson prose is original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Mandate of Heaven
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports that the Zhou (c. 1046-256 BCE) introduced the Mandate of Heaven as a divine right to rule carrying a moral obligation, that Heaven could withdraw the mandate from an unjust ruler, and that the doctrine legitimized dynastic change for centuries. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Han Dynasty
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports Han dates (202 BCE-220 CE; Western Han 202 BCE-9 CE, Eastern Han 25-220 CE), founding by the commoner Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu), the opening of the Silk Road under Emperor Wu (c. 130 BCE; envoy Zhang Qian 138-126 BCE), and paper-making by Cai Lun in 105 CE. Its loose listing of 'the compass' among Han inventions is cross-checked and qualified against the compass reference below.

sourceRecords.title: Shang Dynasty
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports Shang dates (c. 1600-1046 BCE), bronze casting and ritual vessels, oracle-bone divination and script appearing at Anyang c. 1250 BCE, high-quality silk textiles, and the fall of the Shang to King Wu of Zhou at the Battle of Muye in 1046 BCE. Facts synthesized only.

sourceRecords.title: Oracle Bone Script (甲骨文)
sourceRecords.provider: Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art (Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery)
sourceRecords.notes: Museum educational page. Read via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200) after the WebFetch call returned 403. Supports that oracle-bone script (jiaguwen), the earliest known form of systematic Chinese writing, dates from the fourteenth to eleventh century BCE and originated in carving divination texts on tortoise shells and animal bones used to predict future events for the ruler.

sourceRecords.title: History of the compass (lodestone divination to magnetic navigation)
sourceRecords.notes: Used only to qualify the compass chronology, not as a sole source for any standalone claim. Supports the distinction between early Chinese lodestone divination instruments (Han era) and the magnetic needle compass documented for navigation by the Song dynasty (Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays, 1088). This nuance is corroborated by the general historical consensus reflected in the search results reviewed.
